newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian coca farmers agree to end protests.
newsitem.headline: Colombian coca farmers agree to end protests.

text.p: Thousands of peasant farmers agreed to end protests against the government's drug crop eradication program on Thursday after officials promised that small coca plantations would not be forcibly destroyed for the time being.

Tens of thousands of peasants have filled highways and streets around Florencia, capital of southern Caqueta province, since late July to protest against the spraying of local coca crops with herbicide.
A dozen protesters have been killed in clashes with security forces in Caqueta and in similar protests that ended last month in neighboring Putumayo province.
The government, under heavy pressure from Washington to wipe out vast tracts of coca and opium poppy this year, has insisted that it will continue spraying them with herbicide.

But Carlos Enrique Gallego, head of the government's anti-drug office, conceded that Thursday's agreement halting the protests in Caqueta would suspend fumigation of small coca leaf plantations, at least temporarily.

"The government's overall eradication policy will not be suspended," Gallego told Caracol radio network. "Nonetheless, people who submit to a voluntary eradication program that has been proposed to community leaders will not be the target of forcible eradication," he said.

Gallego said the government had agreed to pay farmers the coca plantations that they destroy voluntarily. But he added that a final agreement had not been hammered out on that point because peasants were demanding large payments than government officials have been authorized to offer so far.
"We hope to have an agreement with respect to the value within the next few days," he said.
Colombia is the world's largest exporter of cocaine, which is produced by refining ground coca leaves with chemicals in clandestine drug laboratories scattered across the country.
Colombia was also described as a leading supplier of heroin to the United States in a report issued last week by the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration.
